Section 3
Tuesday, Nov. 2, 1937
Dear Family:
If I remember correctly this letter was started with the statement
that we were embarking on a trip which might prove exeiting. Porbably I too was
a victim of newspaper stories which depict a war torn Chine, the air filled with
Japanese planes raining bombs on defenceless Chinese cities.
As a matter of fact
we flew across 600 miles of China skies from Hongkong to Hankow without seeing a
Japanese plane - and now after more than a week in war torn China we have yet to
experience an air raid
on see any signs of the war. Even here at Nanking where
hundreds of bombs have been dropped it is difficult to find any trace of damage.
This morning we had an air raid alarm but soon the "all cleer"
signal was given
and no planes or bombs were heard.
Wed. Nov. 3rd. No # excitement today except one air raid alarm.
Walked over to
the Embassy office across
the road from Ir. Peck's home and in-
spected the U. S. dug out - very muddy - dark and full of mosquitos.
Think when
the raids come I'll take my chances outside. A direct hit will get you either
in or out of that hole in the ground. If you are outside and lie flat you are
just about as well off and lots more @ mfottable.
Bond left tonight by motor
car for Shanghai. Many cars are constantly going back and forth mostly at
night in order to avoid Jap airplanes machine-gunning them on the road.
friend of ours left his car as a plane approsched and ran out into a field where
there was a Chinese grave mound.
The plane dove at him but he stayed in the lee
of the mound until it passed - then he noticed the Jap turn and come back at him
so he ran around the other side of
the mound - again in the lee.
This perfor-
mance was repeated during six attacks, after which the Jap flew off probably out
of ammunition. I hope Bond doesn't have any such experience.
He is coming back
on Sunday. In the meantime I am working on a lot of reports and proposals re-
quested by the Chinese officials with whom we are trying to deal. If patience
is a virtue we are among the most virtuous alive.
Thursday Nov. 4th. Rained hard all day. Low ceiling no possibility
of airraid. News from Shanghai very bad.
Have been pounding typewriter all day
bearing in mind Mr. Ball's admonition to his Secretary,
"Miss Ella go slow be-
cause I'm in a helluva hurry". There is absolutely no chance of getting a re-
liable typist in Nanking - all the Embassy people are writing their own letters
and those who know how to operate a typewriter are fortunate.
Bond radioed over CNAC system this morning that he arrived at Shanghai
safely without incident.
Mr. Peck is having a farewell dinner for Ar. Holm tonight.
Friday, Nov. 5th. Nice party last night with two ladies present -
a rare occurrence in Nanking these days.
Mr. and Mrs. Richie, No. 1 foreigner
in the Post Office, Mr. Holm, Mr. and Mrs. MoDaniel, a newspaper man and Ambas-
sador Johnson. Today has been another rainy da with low ceiling.
Have been
here a week with not a single air raid. Ordinarily s week of re ny weather is
hard to take but here ax a bright sunny day is ushered in with curses. Have to
see ore
of the Secretaries of the Ministry of Finance tomorrow.
tration building was bon ed and while not badly damaged they are all & reid to
go back and are now quartered in the Ministry of Railways building temporarily
while a bomb proof air conditioned concrete underground office is being onstructed
next door to the American Embassy.
Saturday Nov. 6th. Another low overcast rainy day. When we were
trying to operate a regular airline such stretches of weather were the bane of
our existence..
This weather is all the more remarkable for the fall is usually
the only good weather season in this section of China.
Today I was grateful for
that low ceiling as I had to spend the morning in the Ministry of Railways Bldg.
itself normally the target for bombe attacks located as it is on the main street
with the $12,000,000 Ministry of Communications Bldg. just across the street but
even more of a target now because shared by two other Ministrys, Finance and
